passage:
Thursday
Headache again, the third this week. It starts behind my eyes after school, and by evening it's like a band squeezing my head. I skipped Sana's birthday because the music would have made it worse, and now the group thinks I'm stuck-up. At dinner Chachu said, 'Teenagers and their dramas. It's nothing.' I went to my room and cried, which made it worse.
Then Urmila Khala knocked. She sat on my bed, didn't say anything silly, just asked when it started and what helps. She said, 'Pain that keeps coming back deserves a proper check-up. We'll go to the doctor on Saturday.' I felt so relieved I almost cried again.
Zeenat

qa.q: When will Zeenat and Urmila Khala go to the doctor?
qa.a: On Saturday.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when Chachu called it drama?
qa.a: Zeenat felt hurt and misunderstood, so upset that crying made the headache worse.

qa.q: What did Urmila Khala do that helped?
qa.a: She listened calmly, asked when it started and what helps, and arranged a proper check-up.

qa.q: How might the friends see Zeenat skipping the birthday?
qa.a: They may see Zeenat as stuck-up, not knowing the headache made the music unbearable.

grounding: A teenager with frequent headaches avoids plans and feels dismissed until an adult takes it seriously and arranges a check-up.

subtype: Friend of someone in constant pain [Receiver]
passage:
Sunday night
Urmila cancelled again, the third time this month. We'd planned the film for two weeks, and at five she sent: 'Sorry, bad pain day, can't.' When I asked if she was sure, she replied, 'Yes, Samir. I'm sure.' Full stop. Ouch. I sat on the hostel steps feeling like I didn't matter.
Then I remembered her face in the canteen on Friday, grey and tight, and how she kept shifting in her chair. She's lived with this back pain since the accident last year. Of course she's short on patience; she's short on everything. I'm not taking it personally. I texted: 'No worries. Want me to bring the film and some chaat to your room next week instead?' She sent back a heart.
Samir

qa.q: What did Samir offer to bring next week?
qa.a: The film and some chaat to Urmila's room.

qa.q: How did Samir feel after Urmila's curt reply?
qa.a: Samir felt hurt and unimportant, sitting on the hostel steps as if not mattering.

qa.q: What helped Samir respond kindly?
qa.a: Remembering Urmila's grey face and shifting in the chair, and understanding that pain drains patience, so it wasn't personal.

qa.q: What might Urmila have felt when Samir offered to come to her room?
qa.a: She likely felt relieved and cared for, sending a heart instead of more apologies.

grounding: A friend of someone in constant pain feels hurt by cancelled plans and curt replies, then chooses understanding over offence.

passage:
Counsellor's session note, Shreya, week 4
Shreya arrived late and irritable, snapping that 'these sessions won't fix my joints anyway.' Then she cried. She has lived with joint pain for two years and talks about the dance career she had planned as if it has died. She is exhausted, angry at her body and feels guilty for snapping at her mother. We talked about pacing: breaking her day into short blocks with rest, instead of pushing hard on good days and crashing after. She agreed to tell her mother honestly how the pain feels, and to keep her appointment with her specialist next week. She left calmer. We will continue weekly.
Payal

qa.q: What did Shreya say about the sessions?
qa.a: That 'these sessions won't fix my joints anyway.'

qa.q: What is Shreya grieving, and how does she feel about it?
qa.a: She is grieving the dance career she had planned, and feels exhausted, angry at her body and guilty for snapping at her mother.

qa.q: What plan did Shreya and Payal agree on?
qa.a: Pacing her day in short blocks with rest, telling her mother honestly about the pain, and keeping the specialist appointment.

qa.q: How might Shreya's mother experience the snapping?
qa.a: Her mother may feel hurt or helpless, not knowing how much the pain drains Shreya until they talk honestly.

grounding: A counsellor notes a young woman whose long-lasting pain brings exhaustion, anger and grief, and supports pacing, honesty and medical care.

passage: In the physiotherapy clinic's waiting room, Anand sat beside his husband, Ujjwal, who was shifting on the plastic chair, jaw tight. 'What would help right now?' Anand asked. 'Nothing. Stop asking,' Ujjwal snapped. A woman opposite raised her eyebrows. Anand didn't argue or sulk. He only said, 'Okay. I'm here,' and fetched a cushion from the reception desk. Ujjwal took it without a word, then after a while muttered, 'Sorry. It's bad today.' 'I believe you,' Anand said. That evening Anand's sister took over dinner and the drive home, and Anand went for his usual Thursday swim. He came back rested, not resentful.

qa.q: What did Anand fetch from the reception desk?
qa.a: A cushion.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal snap 'Stop asking'?
qa.a: He was in pain and irritable, so even kind questions felt like pressure, though he later felt sorry.

qa.q: How does Anand keep care from turning into resentment?
qa.a: His sister takes over dinner and the drive home, and he keeps his Thursday swim, so he comes back rested.

qa.q: How might the woman opposite have seen the exchange?
qa.a: She may have thought Ujjwal was rude, without seeing that Anand understood the pain behind the words.

grounding: A partner asks what helps, believes the person in pain, does not take irritability as rejection and protects his own rest.

passage: In their small Vancouver flat, Nadia, hot and flushed, would not let her dad, Chen, put her down. She pushed away her blocks, cried when he reached for a tissue and wailed if he even stood up. So Chen sat on the sofa and held her, humming, one hand on her back. Every so often he checked: was she drinking? Was she breathing easily? When she grew floppier by evening, he phoned the doctor's after-hours line and did what they advised. Nadia slept on his chest, clutching his shirt.

qa.q: Where did Chen sit with Nadia?
qa.a: On the sofa.

qa.q: Why did Nadia cry whenever Chen stood up?
qa.a: She felt ill and frightened and needed the comfort of being held; clinging was her way of seeking it.

qa.q: What was wise about Chen's approach?
qa.a: He gave calm closeness while checking for warning signs, and phoned the doctor's line when she grew floppier.

qa.q: How might Chen have felt holding Nadia all day?
qa.a: Chen was probably tired and anxious yet tender, staying close while watching for danger signs.

grounding: A feverish toddler clings for comfort, and her father gives calm closeness while watching for warning signs.

passage: Dolma had been sick with a cough and fever for three days. She was proud of drinking from a big-girl cup, but now she asked for her old baby bottle from the cupboard. She talked in a squeaky baby voice and crawled into Preeti's bed every night. Her aunt laughed, 'Such a big girl, acting like a baby!' Dolma hid her face. Preeti said gently, 'She's poorly. It's fine,' and filled the bottle with warm water. A week later, fever gone, Dolma pushed the bottle away herself. 'That's for babies.'

qa.q: What did Dolma ask for from the cupboard?
qa.a: Her old baby bottle.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel when her aunt laughed at her?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hurt, and hid her face.

qa.q: Why was Preeti's response wise?
qa.a: Preeti treated the baby behaviour as normal during illness, without shaming, and it faded as Dolma recovered.

qa.q: How might the aunt see Dolma's baby voice?
qa.a: The aunt sees silly babyish behaviour, not a sick child seeking comfort.

grounding: A sick young child goes back to a bottle and baby talk, and it fades on recovery without shaming.

subtype: Sibling annoyed by the sick child's attention [Receiver]
passage: When Ritu got chickenpox last summer, the whole house turned around her. Mummy made her special khichdi, Papa brought her comics, and Nani sat by her bed all day. Nobody asked about my cricket match. I felt invisible. So one morning I said my stomach hurt too and I couldn't go to school. Mummy looked at me for a long time. She didn't scold. That evening she said, 'Pranav, come, just you and me,' and we went for ice cream on the scooter, only us two. She asked about my match, and I told her about my catch. When we got home, I even took Ritu a comic myself.

qa.q: What did Mummy make for Ritu?
qa.a: Special khichdi.

qa.q: Why did Pranav say the stomach hurt too?
qa.a: Pranav felt invisible and resentful with all the attention on Ritu, and wanted some care too.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Pranav?
qa.a: She didn't scold, but gave Pranav one-on-one time on the scooter and asked about the match.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt when Pranav brought a comic?
qa.a: Ritu probably felt pleased and cared for by her sibling, not only by the adults.

grounding: A healthy child resents the fuss over a sick sibling and fakes symptoms, and one-on-one time shows they are still seen.

subtype: Ill teen feeling foggy and cranky [Actor]
passage: Last month I had flu for a week, and I've never felt so stupid. My body felt like wet sand. I tried to revise for the unit test from bed and read the same paragraph ten times. Then I started worrying I'd fail and fall behind forever. When my brother Suraj came in to ask about his cricket bat, I screamed at him and threw a pillow. Ammi made me put the books away. 'Your brain is sick too, Farida. Decide nothing, argue nothing, just rest.' I slept for two days. The test got moved, and I apologised to Suraj once I could think again. His bat was under my bed.

qa.q: Where was Suraj's cricket bat?
qa.a: Under the bed.

qa.q: What was Farida worried about while ill?
qa.a: Farida felt anxious about failing the unit test and falling behind forever.

qa.q: What did Ammi advise, and why was it wise?
qa.a: To decide nothing, argue nothing and just rest, because illness dulls thinking and mood.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when the pillow flew at him?
qa.a: He probably felt shocked and hurt, since he had only asked about his bat.

grounding: A teenager with flu feels foggy and short-tempered and worries about school, and learns to leave decisions and arguments until recovery.

passage: Ojas, before you leave for your hostel, let your Sarika Bua tell you one thing. In my second year at college in Pune, I caught a fever in the monsoon. I lay in my room for two days, shivering, eating dry biscuits, crying for my mother's rasam. I didn't tell anyone. Why bother the warden, I thought, why worry Amma two hundred kilometres away? On the third morning my roommate Kavita found me too weak to stand. She fetched the warden, who took me to the doctor that same hour and phoned Amma. Amma came on the evening bus. I felt foolish for waiting. So promise me: if you're sick, you tell a friend, the warden or us on the very first day.

qa.q: What did young Sarika eat while ill?
qa.a: Dry biscuits.

qa.q: Why didn't young Sarika tell anyone she was sick?
qa.a: She felt reluctant to bother the warden or worry Amma, even while homesick and crying for her mother's rasam.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Sarika's hostel story?
qa.a: Kavita finding her and fetching the warden, who took her to the doctor and phoned Amma the same hour.

qa.q: How might Kavita have felt finding Sarika too weak to stand?
qa.a: Kavita was probably alarmed and worried, which is why she fetched the warden at once.

grounding: An aunt recalls being sick alone in a hostel, homesick and reluctant to bother anyone, and urges reaching out early.

passage:
Tuesday, 11 pm
Stupid, stupid day. Woke up with a fever and a scratchy throat but went in anyway, because missing the sprint review would make me look unreliable. By noon I'd pasted the wrong figures into the client deck and had to redo half of it. Reena covered for me in the meeting, then pulled me aside. 'You're burning up. And half the floor will catch this now.' She was right; Kunal was already sneezing. The manager sent me home at two. I felt ashamed, not of being ill, but of pretending I wasn't. Tomorrow I'm staying home, and I've already messaged the team. If the fever keeps going, I'll see the doctor.
Yogesh

qa.q: What mistake did Yogesh make by noon?
qa.a: Pasted the wrong figures into the client deck.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh go to work with a fever?
qa.a: Yogesh was afraid that missing the sprint review would look unreliable.

qa.q: What is Yogesh doing differently tomorrow?
qa.a: Staying home, having already told the team, and seeing the doctor if the fever keeps going.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt watching Yogesh work while ill?
qa.a: Reena was probably worried and a bit annoyed, covering in the meeting and seeing colleagues at risk of catching it.

grounding: A young professional works with a fever out of fear of seeming unreliable, makes mistakes and spreads illness, then chooses rest.
